newsitem.title: USA: Sports Illustrated to test women's magazine.
newsitem.headline: Sports Illustrated to test women's magazine.

text.p: Sports Illustrated, looking to capitalize on what it believes is an untapped market, said Monday it will test a new magazine devoted to women athletes.
The new magazine, which has the working title of "Sports Illustrated Woman," is to be published twice in 1997 and will debut in April. Future issues will be determined later.

Although there is a plethora of magazines geared to female readers that are devoted to general health and fitness issues, Sports Illustrated said there is a dearth of magazines for women interested in sports -- and news about female athletes.

That includes Sports Illustrated magazine, which is jammed with news about male athletes and the sports they play, football, baseball, basketball and the like. Although the publication has increased its news about women in sports, it remains geared largely to a male audience.
Of Sports Illustrated's 23 million readers, an estimated five million are women. Sports Illustrated is published by Time Inc, a subsidiary of Time Warner Inc.

"Sports Illustrated is not a magazine that carries a tremendous amount of news about female athletes," said Sandy Bailey, the Olympics editor at Sports Illustrated who is coordinating the editorial effort to launch a women's version.
"It's not that easy to get stories in there on female athletes," she said in a telephone interview with Reuters. "Now is the time to test the concept to see if there's a market for it."
The April issue will feature more than 100 pages. The first press run is expected to be about 600,000 copies at a newstand price of $2.95, it said.
The initial distribution includes Sports Illustrated's 450,000 female subscribers, women selected from Time Warner's database and a projected newsstand draw of about 150,000, it said.
The new publication comes at a time when women's sports appear to be gaining momentum, including the creation of a professional women's basketball league.

"With the growing interest in women's sports, the development of new professional leagues and the vast numbers of women who participate in and actively watch sports, we feel the time for this magazine is perfect," Sports Illustrated Associate Publisher John Jay said.
Bailey said the magazine will not necessarily ignore male athletes. And she also does not see the magazine running articles solely on professional sports.
The publication is to be geared toward an audience of women, ages 18 to 34.
Bailey said she is not sure yet what kind of feedback Sports Illustrated Woman will have to receive to be deemed a success worthy of continued publication.
"I'm not sure it's (something) that's been answered here internally," she said.
